Job losses: how many people are losing jobs

How many people are losing jobs. State UI initial claims are the fastest signal, published every Thursday; payrolls, JOLTS and the household survey confirm it monthly. Claims are applications under state rules: a guide to direction and timing.

SA initial claims rate

New job losses. For involuntary unemployment insurance (IUI), this is the public guide to how often claims start (frequency).

Initial claims rate (4-week average), per 10,000 covered workers
What-if pathToday+13 weeks+26 weeks+52 weeksPeak
2001-type12.714.316.620.020.3 after 51 weeks
2008-type12.713.514.920.824.6 after 61 weeks

Each path takes what the series did after the last month before that downturn began and applies it to today's level (unemployment: the same change in points; claims: the same percentage change). A what-if, not a forecast.

No forecast is shown: in testing we could not predict new claims better than assuming no change. The what-if paths show past downturns from today's level.

In the early-warning score, new claims (vs. their 52-week low) are currently the largest downward pull.

We don't show a forecast range for initial claims: in testing it was no more accurate than assuming no change. The early-warning score (Overview, Outlook) is our forward view of new claims.

Source and method

Plotted: 4-week average (bold), weekly (faint). Source: DOL state UI claims (ETA 539 weekly report and Thursday news release; FRED ICSA for preliminary weeks). Seasonally adjusted initial claims per 10,000 covered workers, weekly, from 1971. Hollow markers: preliminary. Grey bands: NBER recessions. Dotted lines: average SA weekly rate over the 12 months up to each NBER peak (Apr 2000–Mar 2001, Jan–Dec 2007, Mar 2019–Feb 2020) and over 2019. Last data: Nov 21, 2026, preliminary (advance). What-if paths repeat the 2001 and 2008 recessions from the latest 4-week average; they are not forecasts. Forecast elements appear only when the time range includes today.

SA initial claims

Week-to-week detail on new claims; the 4-week average smooths holiday and weather noise.

Plotted: 4-week average (bold), weekly (faint). Source: DOL state UI claims via FRED (ICSA, IC4WSA). Seasonally adjusted, number of claims, weekly. Hollow markers: preliminary. Grey bands: NBER recessions. Last data: Nov 21, 2026, preliminary (advance).

NSA initial claims: this year vs. the prior 3 years

Raw claims follow a strong seasonal pattern; comparing years checks the seasonal adjustment.

Fixed view: by week of year, whatever the time setting.

Source and method

Source: DOL state UI claims (ETA 539 weekly report and Thursday news release). Not seasonally adjusted, number of claims, weekly, by week-ending date. Fixed view: ignores the page time control. Hollow markers: preliminary. Last data: Nov 21, 2026, preliminary (advance).

Initial claims vs. a year ago

Turns the claims level into a trend: above zero means claims are running higher than a year ago.

Source: DOL state UI claims via FRED (IC4WSA). Percent change in the SA 4-week average vs. the same week 52 weeks earlier, weekly. Hollow markers: preliminary. Grey bands: NBER recessions. Last data: Nov 21, 2026, preliminary (advance).

Payroll change

Net jobs added or lost each month: the broadest monthly measure of hiring minus job losses. Payroll change is net (hiring minus separations), so layoffs can rise while payrolls still grow.

Source: BLS Current Employment Statistics via FRED (PAYEMS). Monthly change in total nonfarm payrolls, thousands of jobs, seasonally adjusted. Grey bands: NBER recessions. Last data: Oct 2026.

JOLTS layoffs and discharges rate

Layoffs reported by employers, including those that never lead to an unemployment claim.

Source: BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey via FRED (JTSLDR). Layoffs and discharges as a percent of total employment, seasonally adjusted, monthly; JOLTS starts Dec 2000. Grey bands: NBER recessions. Last data: Sep 2026.

Newly unemployed (less than 5 weeks)

A proxy for fresh inflow into unemployment, from the household survey, whether or not people file a claim.

Source: BLS Current Population Survey via FRED (UEMPLT5). Number unemployed less than 5 weeks, thousands, seasonally adjusted, monthly. Gap: no October 2025 survey (government shutdown). Grey bands: NBER recessions. Last data: Oct 2026.

Unemployed by reason: permanent vs. temporary layoff

Permanent layoffs become long claims; temporary layoffs usually end in recall. A rise in the permanent line is the more serious sign for claim frequency and severity.

Source: BLS Current Population Survey via FRED (LNS13026638, LNS13023653). Thousands of persons, seasonally adjusted, monthly; permanent job losers from 1994. Gap: no October 2025 survey. Grey bands: NBER recessions. Last data: Oct 2026.

Private payrolls: ADP vs. BLS

A second, independent read on private jobs; useful when the BLS jobs report is delayed (as in the October 2025 shutdown).

Source and method

Sources: ADP National Employment Report via FRED (ADPMNUSNERSA) and BLS Current Employment Statistics via FRED (USPRIV). Monthly change in private nonfarm payrolls, thousands of jobs, seasonally adjusted, from 2010. ADP is built from payroll records of ADP clients and published two days before the BLS report. Outside 2020-21 the two differ by about 55k jobs in a typical month and by 100k or more in 3 months out of 10. Context only: not used in the early-warning score. Grey bands: NBER recessions. Last data: Oct 2026.

Not an official forecast; public data only. Figures are revised by their publishers; this site shows the latest published values and refreshes automatically on weekday mornings.

Sources: U.S. Department of Labor, Employment and Training Administration (weekly claims, ETA 539); U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics and Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis via FRED (unemployment rate, Sahm indicator, claims); National Bureau of Economic Research recession dates via FRED (USREC); leading indicators from the U.S. Treasury, U.S. Census Bureau, Federal Reserve Banks of Philadelphia, New York and Chicago, and the University of Michigan Surveys of Consumers, via FRED (each chart names its source); release schedules from FRED and the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago.
